title: A small book, everywhere
hookLine: a grandmother's prayer book with a cracked spine: The Imitation of Christ opens, a book that never assumes you've arrived
tomorrow: what does it mean to follow someone, not just copy them?

lines: A CRACKED SPINE. HALF THE LINES UNDERLINED.
cards: A grandmother's prayer book with a cracked spine. A paperback in a gym bag with half its lines underlined. Small books go places big ones can't: a jacket pocket, a nightstand drawer, a hospital waiting room.
The book that opens on this path today is that kind. The Imitation of Christ. Short chapters, plain sentences, nothing to prove.

teach.b: So what makes a book for beginners worth carrying for life?
Tradition credits The Imitation of Christ to Thomas à Kempis, a canon in a religious house in what's now the Netherlands, and says he wrote it for the novices joining his community.
It takes its name from its first chapter's heading, on imitating Christ. It doesn't build a system. It gives counsel, one saying at a time.

And its answer to the question is in its first chapter: it never lets you think you've arrived. What good is it, it asks, to argue deeply about the Trinity if you lack humility and so displease the Trinity?

teach.h: LIVE IT BEFORE YOU KNOW IT.
teach.b: Living it comes before knowing about it. That's one to tell a friend tonight. Here's a neighbor who'd recognize the shape.
Judaism has a small book of sayings too, Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, in the Mishnah. One of its sages asks: who is wise? And answers: the one who learns from every person.
Both books prize a learner who stays a beginner, and both are meant to be lived, a line at a time.

teach.h: A CHAIN OF SAGES, ONE VOICE.
teach.b: And an honest difference: Pirkei Avot opens with a chain, Moses receiving the Torah at Sinai and handing it on, teacher to teacher, and its sayings belong to named sages living the Torah.
The Imitation speaks in one unnamed voice, to a reader learning to follow Christ.

how: Some Catholics keep a copy of The Imitation of Christ by the bed or in a bag and read a chapter at a time as spiritual reading.

s: The Imitation of Christ is a thick theology textbook for experts
it's short chapters of plain counsel, written for beginners.
its first chapter puts humility ahead of arguing about the Trinity
what good is deep argument, it asks, if you lack humility?
Pirkei Avot and the Imitation say the same thing in different words
both prize the lifelong learner; Avot hands on named sages' Torah teaching, the Imitation follows Christ.

games.q: a Jewish classmate shows you her small, worn copy of Pirkei Avot, the sayings she studies. what's an honest thing to say?
o: both books prize a learner who stays a beginner; hers hands on named sages, yours follows Christ.
they're basically the same book, just with different names on the cover.
nothing about the books, since mentioning two faiths at once is rude.
games.why: the shared thing is real: a small book of sayings to be lived, and a love of learning from everyone. so is the difference. naming both honors both.

practice: Pick up one small book that matters to you, a prayer book, a worn paperback, anything with short lines, and open it anywhere. Read one paragraph, slowly, once, the way a beginner would, and then rest your eyes on the page.

wordCard.voice: A small book. The Imitation of Christ: short counsel for beginners, written to be lived a line at a time.

orig.note: Latin: of the imitation of Christ, the book's title, from its first chapter's heading.

carryVoice: Keep this one: a book for beginners, which turns out to mean everyone, every time they open it. See you tomorrow.
